title: Real-Time, Two-Color Stimulated Raman Scattering Imaging of Mouse Brain for Tissue Diagnosis
protocol: Install a pair of achromatic lenses for the pump beam.
Use a 100 mm lens and 200 mm lens to magnify the laser beam size by 2-fold.
Ensure that the distance between the two lenses is roughly 300 mm.
Align the pump beam through the center of both lenses.
Place a mirror after the second lens to send the beam toward a wall (>1 m away).
Take care when sending the beam across long distances.
Trace the beam from the mirror to the wall with an IR card.
Check if the beam changes in size.
Collimate the beam if the beam changes in size as a function of distance.
Move the two lenses closer if the beam is converging (decreasing size with propagation).
Move the two lenses further apart if the beam is diverging (increasing size with propagation).
Adjust the distance until the beam is collimated.
Repeat steps for the Stokes beam to collimate the beam.
Measure the collimated beam size for each beam if a beam profiler is available.
Estimate the beam size using the IR card and a ruler to obtain a beam diameter of 4-5 mm.
Change the lens pair used in step 1.1 if the beam size is too small or too large.
Adjust the lens pair until both beams have a diameter of 4-5 mm.
Combine the two laser beams using a dichroic mirror.
Install steering mirrors for adjustment of the laser beams.
Monitor the pump and Stokes beams after the dichroic mirror at two positions, approximately 1 meter apart.
Iteratively adjust the steering mirror before the dichroic to align the Stokes beam with the pump beam.
Adjust the dichroic mirror iteratively until both beams are spatially overlapping at both monitoring positions.
Ensure that both combined beams pass through the center of the scan mirrors when parked.
Place a pair of steering mirrors after the condenser to ensure both beams travel through the center of the microscope objective and condenser.
Relay the transmitted beam onto the photodiode using a lens with a focal length of 100 mm followed by another lens with a 30 mm focal length.
Ensure that both beams are contained within the photodiode for detection.
Install two low-pass filters to block out the modulated Stokes beam.
Place a beam sampler in the Stokes beam path to pick up 10% of the beam and send it to a fast photodiode to detect the 80 MHz pulse train.
Send the photodiode signal to a frequency divider to generate a 20 MHz TTL output.
Further send the TTL output into a fanout buffer to replicate the output into four identical 20 MHz outputs.
Use one of the outputs from the fanout buffer and filter it with a bandpass filter to get a 20 MHz sinusoidal wave.
Adjust the filtered output peak-to-peak voltage to ~500 mV using an RF attenuator.
Send the resulting output to a phase shifter.
Connect the phase shifter output to an RF power amplifier.
Connect the amplifier output to the EOM.
Unblock the Stokes beam and place a photodiode in its path.
Adjust the EOM voltage.
Adjust the quarter-wave plate until modulation depth appears satisfactory.
Monitor temporal overlap with an oscilloscope.
Block the Stokes beam and unblock the pump beam.
Zoom in on one of the pump pulse peaks using the oscilloscope.
Mark the peak position with a vertical cursor.
Block the pump beam and unblock the Stokes beam.
Translate the delay stage to match the Stokes beam peak position with the marked position.
Move the delay stage to the middle of its movement range if necessary.
Calculate the delay distance required by multiplying the temporal difference between the two beams by the speed of light.
Elongate the beam path of the faster beam or shorten the beam path of the slower beam accordingly.
Prepare a microscope slide sample with DMSO and double-sided tape as a spacer.
Place the sample on the microscope with the coverslip side facing the objective.
Change to brightfield illumination and observe the sample from the eyepiece.
Find the focus at both the top and bottom layer of air bubbles at the glass-tape interface.
Move the focus to be in between the two layers of tape.
Ensure laser beams are blocked before looking into the eyepiece.
Set the tunable beam output to 798 nm.
Adjust the optical power to be ~40 mW each for the pump and Stokes beams at the objective focus.
Open ScanImage in MATLAB or other scanning software that controls the microscope.
Click on the button labeled FOCUS to start scanning.
Adjust the steering mirror before the galvo scanner to center the DC signal on channel 1 display.
Move the motorized delay stage and observe the lock-in output shown on channel 2 (AC channel) display.
Fine-tune the time delay to maximize the AC signal intensity when pump and Stokes coincide in time.
Adjust the dichroic mirror to center the SRS signal on the AC channel while keeping the DC channel centered.
Maximize the signal by adjusting the phase of the lock-in amplifier.
Insert 48 cm of a highly dispersive glass rod into the 800 nm beam path.
Estimate the GDD using Eq (1).
Calculate how many cm of the dispersive glass rod is required for the 1,040 nm beam path to match the GDD of the pump.
Insert the appropriate length of dispersive glass rods to the 1,040 nm beam path to roughly match the GDD of the 800 nm beam.
Adjust the temporal overlap of the two beams as necessary.
Make a microscope slide sample with DMSO.
Place the slide onto the microscope and check the power of the beams coming out of the microscope condenser.
Adjust the power accordingly to have ~40 mW each at sample focus.
Open ScanImage from MATLAB.
Scan through the delay stage to find the maximal SRS signal corresponding to the 2,913 cm-1 Raman peak of DMSO.
Estimate the new stage position based on previous data with the increased optical path length due to added rods.
Realign the beam spatial overlap to account for deviations caused by glass rod insertion.
Save a hyperspectral SRS scan by sequentially taking series of SRS images while moving the motorized stage.
Plot out the SRS spectra of the DMSO solution using ImageJ or MATLAB.
Fit the large 2,913 cm-1 peak to a Gaussian or Lorentzian function in MATLAB to calculate FWHM.
NOTE: A good SNR for the system using DMSO at 40 mw/40 mw is >800.
Adjust DMSO concentration or power if data acquisition card has limited bit depth.
Realign laser pulses if SNR is too low, optimizing spatial overlap, temporal overlap, beam size/collimation matching, and dispersion matching.
Optimize signal by adjusting aberration correction collar for objective with an aberration correction collar.
Save a hyperspectral scan covering the 2,913 cm-1 and 2,994 cm-1 Raman peaks of DMSO.
Save stage positions corresponding to the hyperspectral dataset.
Perform linear regression for the stage positions and Raman shifts at 2,913 cm-1.
Perform linear regression for the stage positions and Raman shifts at 2,994 cm-1.
Convert the delay positions to corresponding Raman frequencies using the linear regression equation relating stage position to Raman shift.
Install a PBS (PBS2) into the Stokes beam path after the first EOM.
Install a quarter-wave plate (QWP2) into the Stokes beam path after PBS2.
Install a second EOM (EOM2) into the Stokes beam path after QWP2.
Unplug the signal input to EOM2.
Plug in the signal input to EOM1 and turn it on.
Modulate the Stokes beam (fixed at 1,040 nm) at 20 MHz by sending through EOM1.
Adjust the tilt of EOM1 to ensure the beam hits straight and centered through the crystal.
Adjust the position of EOM1 to ensure the beam hits straight and centered through the crystal.
Monitor modulation depth by observing both polarizations coming out of PBS1 with two photodiodes.
Display modulation on an oscilloscope.
Adjust QWP1, EOM1 voltage, and phase of the 20 MHz input to optimize modulation depth close to 100%.
Unplug EOM1 and plug in EOM2.
Send high voltage output from the second amplifier at 20 MHz to EOM2.
Tilt and position EOM2 to ensure beam hits straight and centered through the crystal.
Monitor modulation depth by looking at both polarizations coming out of PBS2 with an oscilloscope.
Adjust QWP2, EOM2 voltage, and phase shifter as needed to achieve close to 100% modulation for both polarizations.
Ensure pulse train modulation has a 90° phase shift from the first modulation.
Turn on and plug in both EOM1 and EOM2.
Monitor both polarizations being split by PBS2 with an oscilloscope.
Reoptimize EOM1 and EOM2 individually if the pulse train after the second PBS does not resemble Figure 2C.
Install a 20 mm birefringent quartz crystal (BRC) and HWP downstream of EOM2.
Plug in both EOMs at once.
Monitor the pulse train such that it resembles Figure 2D.
Calibrate the system using DMSO by detecting signals from the lock-in amplifier X and Y channel output.
Check whether the signals generated by the 2,913 cm-1 peak from the faster polarization and that from the slower polarization are close to 90° out-of-phase on the lock-in amplifier.
Adjust the EOM alignment until the two signals are close to 90° out-of-phase.
Find the delay position that probes the protein transition at 2,930 cm-1 for one of the orthogonal beams.
Ensure that the other polarization probes the lipid transition of 2,850 cm-1.
Install an HWP before the beam enters the microscope to change the polarization of the beam going into the microscope.
Place a PBS above the objective to allow the depolarized back-reflected beam to reach the detector.
Use a pair of lenses consisting of a 75 mm achromat lens and a 30 mm aspheric lens to relay the backscattered photons from the back aperture of the objective to the photodetector.
Mount the detector to collect the backscattered light directed by the PBS.
Install a filter to block out the modulated beam from entering the detector.
Place the tissue sample under the objective.
Remove the condenser if more space is required for epi-mode imaging.
Block off the beam with a shutter.
Shine a white light source onto the sample from the side using brightfield.
Find objective focus.
Unblock both beams.
Use precalibrated delay positions to acquire lipid SRS images from tissue from one output of the lock-in amplifier.
Use precalibrated delay positions to acquire protein SRS images from tissue from another output of the lock-in amplifier.
Adjust the lock-in gain and pixel bin factor to acquire good-quality images.
Open the image stack with ImageJ.
Right-click on the lipid image (2,850 cm-1) and click Duplicate. Rename this image to lipids.
Right-click on the protein image (2,930 cm-1) and click Duplicate. Rename this image to proteins.
Go to Process | Image Calculator and perform proteins subtract lipids.
Go to Image | Color | Merge Channels. Set lipids to green and proteins to blue.
Open the image channels tool (Image | Color | Channels Tool).
Adjust the brightness and contrast for each channel using the channels tool.
For the lipid channel, adjust the contrast until the cellular features appear dark.
For the protein channel, adjust the contrast until the cellular features appear blue.
Convert the merged channel green/blue image to an RGB image by going to Image | Type | RGB Color.
Export this image by File | Save As | Tiff.
Run the HE.m script in MATLAB.
Select the exported RGB image from the previous step.
Generate an artificially H&E stained image.
Normalize the image intensity for large field-of-view imaging.
Average as many images as possible.
Remove the intensity features with ImageJ using Gaussian Blur (Radius=50).
Measure the maximum intensity of the blurred image.
Divide the blurred image by the maximum intensity.
Divide the raw SRS image by the blurred image.
